hook.situation: Your Korean friend tells you about a stressful day: someone at work was 'pretending not to know,' they 'almost cried' during a movie, and they're 'guessing the boss is angry.' You understand the gist but can't quite follow the grammar gluing it together. Those three reactions — faking something, narrowly avoiding something, and inferring from clues — each need their own structure in Korean.
objectives: Use -는 척하다 to say someone is pretending or faking a state or action
Use -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 to describe a close call — something that almost happened but didn't
Use -나 보다 / -(으)ㄴ가 보다 to make an evidence-based guess about someone else's situation
hook.whyItMatters: These three patterns appear constantly in Korean storytelling and conversation. Without them, you can describe facts but not the texture of human experience — the white lies, the near-misses, and the inferences you draw about the people around you. Master all three and your Korean instantly sounds more natural and more adult.

grammarNotes.title: -는 척하다 — Pretend / Act Like
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of -는 척하다 as putting on a MASK. The person is wearing a mask of something they're not — sleeping, working, not knowing. The mask can be any verb or adjective, and you just need to fit the right modifier ending to the mask before slipping it on. If the mask is an action happening now: -는 척. If the mask is a state (adjective): -은/-ㄴ 척. If you're pretending you already DID something: -(으)ㄴ 척.
grammarNotes.formation:
Action verb (present): verb stem + -는 척하다 (먹다 → 먹는 척하다)
Adjective: stem + -(으)ㄴ 척하다 (아프다 → 아픈 척하다, 바쁘다 → 바쁜 척하다)
Past action: stem + -(으)ㄴ 척하다 (듣다 → 들은 척하다, 보다 → 본 척하다)
척하다 conjugates normally: 척해요, 척했어요, 척할 거예요

examples.en: My boss came so I pretended to be working hard.
examples.note: 일하다 is an action verb → present modifier -는 + 척했어요; the pretense was ongoing in the past

examples.ko: 전 남자친구를 봤는데 못 본 척했어요.
examples.romanization: jeon namjachingureul bwanneunde mot bon cheokaesseoyo.
examples.en: I saw my ex-boyfriend but pretended not to have seen him.
examples.note: 보다 = past completed action → -(으)ㄴ modifier: 본 척 (pretending you already looked away)

examples.en: I pretended to be sick to skip the company dinner.
examples.note: 아프다 is an adjective → -(으)ㄴ modifier: 아픈 척; note the 으 is needed after the consonant stem

examples.romanization: gyae da almyeonseo moreuneun cheokajana yo.
examples.en: She totally knows but acts like she doesn't.
examples.note: 모르다 = action verb (not knowing = an active state of ignorance) → present -는 척; -잖아요 expresses mild exasperation

examples.ko: 전화 안 들리는 척하면 안 돼.
examples.romanization: jeonhwa an deulleuneun cheokhamyeon an dwae.
examples.en: You can't just pretend not to hear the phone.
examples.note: 들리다 = action verb → -는 척; -면 안 돼 = 'you shouldn't' — the pretense is framed as a conditional

b.en: It seems like he's sleeping. (honest impression)

contrastPairs.explanation: Same base phrase, completely different meaning. 척하다 = deliberate faking — you KNOW it's false. -는 것 같다 = a genuine soft opinion. These are opposites in spirit: one is a performance, the other is an honest guess.

a.en: She pretended to be busy. (she wasn't)

contrastPairs.explanation: Again: 척했어요 = the person was actively faking. -것 같았어요 = your sincere impression. When you describe someone else's pretense, use 척하다; when you describe your own perception, use -것 같다.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers apply the action-verb pattern to adjectives. But 아프다 is an adjective, not an action verb, so it takes the adjective modifier -(으)ㄴ, not -는. The result is 아픈 척했어요. This is the most common 척하다 mistake — always check whether your word is an adjective (state) or a verb (action) before choosing the modifier.

exceptions: 체하다 is a less common but valid alternative to 척하다 with the same meaning: 모르는 체했어요 = 모르는 척했어요
Past action pretense uses -(으)ㄴ even for action verbs: 안 들은 척하다 (pretend not to have heard) — don't confuse with the adjective -(으)ㄴ, though the ending looks the same
The contracted spoken form 척하다 → often shortens to just 척 in casual speech: '자, 자는 척!' (Act like you're sleeping!)

grammarNotes.title: -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 — Almost Happened (Close Call)
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 as a NEAR-MISS ALARM. The alarm went off — something was right on the edge of happening — but the disaster was avoided. The alarm is always in the past (뻔했어요) because the near-miss is already over. The adverb 하마터면 is the sound of the alarm: '하마터면...!' = 'I almost...!'
grammarNotes.formation:
Verb stem (vowel or ㄹ-ending): + -ㄹ 뻔하다 (넘어지다 → 넘어질 뻔하다, 울다 → 울 뻔하다)
Verb stem (consonant-ending): + -을 뻔하다 (죽다 → 죽을 뻔하다, 늦다 → 늦을 뻔하다)
Almost always past: 뻔했어요
Optional intensifier: 하마터면 + -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요
Only used with action verbs, not adjectives

examples.en: The road was slippery so I almost fell.
examples.note: 넘어지다 ends in a vowel → -ㄹ 뻔했어요; -아서 gives the cause that nearly triggered the disaster

examples.ko: 하마터면 지하철에 가방을 두고 내릴 뻔했어요.
examples.romanization: hamateomyeon jihacheore gabangeul dugo naeril ppeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I almost left my bag on the subway!
examples.note: 하마터면 at the front = the 'alarm sound'; 내리다 ends in a vowel → -ㄹ 뻔했어요

examples.en: It was so moving I almost cried.
examples.note: 울다 has a ㄹ stem → just -ㄹ 뻔했어요 (the ㄹ in the stem counts); feeling-based near-misses are very natural with this pattern

examples.en: I didn't hear my alarm and almost got to work late.
examples.note: 지각하다 ends in 하 → 지각할 뻔했어요; 하다 verbs follow the vowel rule

examples.ko: 차가 갑자기 튀어나와서 사고 날 뻔했어요.
examples.romanization: chaga gapjagi twieonawaseo sago nal ppeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: A car suddenly darted out and there was almost an accident.
examples.note: 나다 ends in a vowel → -ㄹ 뻔했어요; 사고 나다 = an accident occurs — common pairing with this pattern

a.en: I almost fell. (it genuinely nearly happened)

b.en: It felt like I was going to fall. (my impression at the time)

contrastPairs.explanation: 뻔했어요 = a real near-miss, the event was on the physical edge of happening. -ㄹ 것 같았어요 = your mental impression or fear at the moment. If you're telling a story about a genuine close call, use 뻔했어요. If you're describing how something felt or looked from the outside, use -것 같았어요.

b.en: I feel like I'm going to cry (might still cry).

contrastPairs.explanation: 뻔했어요 is past and the event DIDN'T happen — the danger is over. -ㄹ 것 같아요 is present and the event may still happen. This is a key practical difference.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers try to keep it in the present. But a near-miss, by definition, is already over — so Korean always uses the past form 뻔했어요. 뻔해요 in the present tense sounds unnatural. The one very rare exception is live commentary ('He's about to fall!'), but in normal storytelling you always say 뻔했어요.

exceptions: Rarely used about ongoing or future events; almost exclusively past tense
Not used with adjectives: 피곤할 뻔했어요 (almost tired?) doesn't make sense — only with event verbs
Can be positive: 상을 받을 뻔했어요 (I almost won a prize) — though most near-misses described this way are negative (disasters avoided)

extendedVocabulary.english: deep emotion; being moved or touched

exampleSentence.ko: 그 영화 너무 감동적이어서 울 뻔했어요.
exampleSentence.en: That movie was so moving I almost cried.
exampleSentence.note: 감동적이다 = to be moving/touching; 울 뻔했어요 shows the emotional near-miss naturally

exampleSentence.ko: 그 사람 표정 보니까 두려운가 봐요.
exampleSentence.en: From that person's expression, it seems they're afraid.
exampleSentence.note: 두렵다 (adjective) → -(으)ㄴ가 보다 = evidence-based guess about someone's emotional state

exampleSentence.ko: 팀장님 말투가 그러는 걸 보니까 화나신 건가 봐요.
exampleSentence.en: The way the team leader is talking, I'm guessing they're angry.
exampleSentence.note: -(으)ㄴ가 봐요 = inferring the emotion from observable evidence (their tone)

exampleSentence.ko: 합격했다는 소식을 듣고 만족스러워서 소리를 지를 뻔했어요.
exampleSentence.en: When I heard I passed, I was so satisfied I almost shouted.
exampleSentence.note: 만족스럽다 = to feel satisfied; 소리를 지르다 = to shout; 지를 뻔했어요 = almost-shouted close call

exampleSentence.ko: 그분이 모르는 척한 것 때문에 신뢰를 잃었어요.
exampleSentence.en: Because he pretended not to know, I lost trust in him.
exampleSentence.note: 모르는 척하다 (pretending not to know) combined with 신뢰를 잃다 (lose trust) — common real-life pairing

exampleSentence.ko: 그분이 그렇게 성실한 걸 보니까 존경스러운가 봐요.
exampleSentence.en: Seeing how diligent that person is, they must seem admirable.
exampleSentence.note: 존경스럽다 → -(으)ㄴ가 봐요; guessing someone else's feeling of admiration from their behavior
성실하다 is an adjective → 성실한 것 같다 (soft opinion); contrast with -나 보다 which implies outside evidence

exampleSentence.ko: 그 사람이 모르는 척한 걸 보면 정직한가 싶어요.
exampleSentence.en: Seeing them pretend not to know makes me wonder if they're actually honest.
exampleSentence.note: 모르는 척하다 directly contradicts 정직하다; this contrast appears naturally in character assessments

extendedVocabulary.english: to be careful; prudent; cautious in decisions

exampleSentence.ko: 그 사람 말을 잘 안 하는 걸 보니까 신중한가 봐요.
exampleSentence.en: They don't say much — I'm guessing they're the careful type.
exampleSentence.note: 신중하다 → -(으)ㄴ가 봐요; inferring personality from observable behavior

extendedVocabulary.english: to be coolheaded; level-headed; cold; detached

exampleSentence.en: I pretended to be emotionless, but it was actually tough.
exampleSentence.note: 감정이 없는 척하다 = pretend to be cold/unemotional; 척하다 used for performing emotional detachment

extendedVocabulary.english: tricky; demanding; picky; hard to satisfy

exampleSentence.ko: 심사 기준이 까다로운가 봐요. 다들 탈락했네요.
exampleSentence.en: I guess the judging criteria are strict — everyone got eliminated.
exampleSentence.note: 까다롭다 → -(으)ㄴ가 봐요 (evidence-based inference from the result); ㅂ-irregular: 까다롭 + 은가 → 까다로운가

extendedVocabulary.english: 'I almost...'; by a narrow margin (near-miss adverb)

exampleSentence.note: 하마터면 always pairs with -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 to emphasize the narrowness of the near-miss

extendedVocabulary.english: to pick up on; to sense; to figure out (from cues)

exampleSentence.ko: 걔가 눈치챈 것 같아서 아무것도 모르는 척했어요.
exampleSentence.en: I felt like they were picking up on it, so I pretended not to know anything.
exampleSentence.note: 눈치채다 → trigger for using 척하다: when someone might catch on, you put on the ignorance mask

extendedVocabulary.english: to hide; to conceal (feelings or information)

exampleSentence.en: I pretended to be fine in an attempt to hide my feelings.
exampleSentence.note: 감추려고 (in order to hide) + 척하다 — a very natural Korean expression of masking emotions

extendedVocabulary.english: to be obvious; to show; to give away (that you're faking)

exampleSentence.en: I pretended to be asleep but I guess it was obvious.
exampleSentence.note: 티가 났나 봐요 = evidence-based guess (someone's reaction revealed it); 척하다 + 나 봐요 together in one sentence

extendedVocabulary.english: to tremble; to be shaky (with nerves or emotion)

exampleSentence.en: During my presentation, my voice almost started shaking.
exampleSentence.note: 떨리다 ends in vowel → -ㄹ 뻔했어요; common near-miss emotion verb in presentations and auditions

extendedDialogue.setting: Two coworkers, Jiyeon and Minsu, are eating lunch together and talking about a stressful morning

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 오늘 오전에 발표하다가 목소리가 떨릴 뻔했어요.
lines.romanization: oneul ojeone balpyohada ga moksoriga teollil ppeonhaesseoyo.
lines.en: This morning during my presentation, my voice almost started shaking.
lines.grammarNote: 떨리다 = vowel-stem verb → -ㄹ 뻔했어요; the near-miss is past and already resolved

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 어, 저도 봤는데 엄청 자연스러웠어요. 몰랐어요.
lines.romanization: eo, jeodo bwanneunde eomcheong jayeonseureowoosseoyo. mollasseoyo.
lines.en: Oh, I was watching and you were super natural. I couldn't tell.
lines.grammarNote: No grammar point here — a natural supportive reply that makes the 척하다 line in the next turn more impactful

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 고마워요. 사실 많이 떨렸는데 괜찮은 척했어요.
lines.romanization: gomawoyo. sasil mani teolryeonneunde gwaenchanheun cheokaesseoyo.
lines.en: Thank you. I was actually shaking a lot, but I pretended to be fine.
lines.grammarNote: 괜찮다 is an adjective → -(으)ㄴ 척하다: 괜찮은 척했어요; confirms the mask was successfully worn

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 그래요? 팀장님도 잘 모르시는 것 같던데요.
lines.romanization: geuraeyо? timjangnimdo jal moreusineun geot gatdeondeyo.
lines.en: Really? It seemed like the team leader didn't notice either.
lines.grammarNote: -것 같던데요 = a gentle evidence-based impression recalled from the past; softer than -나 봐요 here because the speaker is recounting their own observation

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 팀장님은 지금 다른 문제로 머리가 복잡한가 봐요.
lines.romanization: timjangnimeun jigeum dareun munjero meoriga bokjapanga bwayo.
lines.en: I think the team leader's head is full of other problems right now.
lines.grammarNote: 복잡하다 = adjective → -(으)ㄴ가 봐요: 복잡한가 봐요; evidence-based inference about someone else's mental state

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 맞아요. 아침에 표정이 안 좋더라고요. 스트레스 많이 받으시나 봐요.
lines.romanization: majayo. achime pyojeongi an jotdeoragoyo. seuteureseu mani badumsina bwayo.
lines.en: Right. The expression this morning wasn't great. I'm guessing they're under a lot of stress.
lines.grammarNote: 받다 = action verb → -나 봐요 (not -(으)ㄴ가); the visible evidence (bad expression) triggers the inference

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 하마터면 제가 먼저 물어볼 뻔했는데 참았어요.
lines.romanization: hamateomyeon jega meonjeo mureоbol ppeonaennneunde chamasseoyo.
lines.en: I almost asked first, but I held back.
lines.grammarNote: 하마터면 + 물어보다 (vowel stem) → -ㄹ 뻔했는데; -는데 adds a contrastive note (almost did, but then...)

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 잘하셨어요. 지금은 모르는 척하는 게 나을 것 같아요.
lines.romanization: jalhaseyosseoyo. jigeumeun moreuneun cheokhaneun ge naeul geot gatayo.
lines.en: Good call. Right now, playing dumb is probably better.
lines.grammarNote: 모르다 = action verb → 모르는 척하다; 하는 게 나을 것 같다 = 'it's probably better to...' — 척하다 appears as a noun-modifying clause here

readingText.title: 지연의 하루 일기 (Jiyeon's Day Diary)
readingText.body: 오늘은 정말 힘든 하루였다. 아침에 중요한 발표가 있었는데, 엄청 긴장해서 울 뻔했다. 발표하는 내내 떨렸지만 괜찮은 척하면서 끝까지 버텼다. 팀장님은 좀 무표정하게 앉아 계셨는데, 뭔가 불만이신가 봐서 마음이 불안했다. 나중에 동료한테 물어봤더니 요즘 윗사람한테 스트레스 받으시나 봐라고 했다. 그 말 듣고 조금 안심이 됐다. 퇴근하다가 지갑을 잃어버릴 뻔했다. 하마터면 큰일 날 뻔했는데, 다행히 가방 안쪽에 있었다. 내일은 오늘보다 나은 하루이길 바란다.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Today was a really tough day. There was an important presentation in the morning, and I was so nervous I almost cried. I was shaking the whole time but I pretended to be fine and hung in there to the end. The team leader sat there with a blank expression, and I felt uneasy thinking they seemed dissatisfied with something. I asked a coworker later, and they said it looks like the team leader has been under stress from upper management lately. Hearing that made me feel a bit relieved. On the way out of the office, I almost lost my wallet. That was almost a disaster, but thankfully it was in the inside pocket of my bag. I hope tomorrow is a better day than today.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Why did Jiyeon pretend to be fine during the presentation?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: She was shaking and almost cried (울 뻔했다), but she put on a mask of composure (괜찮은 척하면서) and pushed through to the end.

comprehensionQuestions.question: How does Jiyeon learn about the team leader's stress? What Korean pattern does she use for this inference?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: She hears it from a coworker. She uses 스트레스 받으시나 봐 — the -나 봐 pattern (action verb 받다 → 받으시나 봐) because the information is secondhand evidence, not something she observed directly.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every instance of 척하다, 뻔하다, and -나/-(으)ㄴ가 보다 in the text. For each one, explain WHY that particular pattern is used there.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 척하다: 괜찮은 척하면서 — she is deliberately performing composure she does not feel (adjective 괜찮다 → -(으)ㄴ 척). 뻔하다: 울 뻔했다 — she genuinely nearly cried (ulda vowel stem → 울 뻔했다); 잃어버릴 뻔했다 — she genuinely almost lost her wallet (잃어버리다 vowel stem → -ㄹ 뻔했다); 큰일 날 뻔했는데 — almost a disaster (나다 vowel stem → -ㄹ 뻔했는데). -나/-(으)ㄴ가 보다: 불만이신가 봐서 — 불만이다 is a 이다 predicate → -인가 봐; vague-evidence inference from a blank expression. 스트레스 받으시나 봐 — 받다 is an action verb → -나 봐; secondhand inference from coworker's information.

culturalNote.title: 척하다 and the Art of Saving Face in Korean Workplaces
culturalNote.body: Korean workplace culture places enormous value on 눈치 (the ability to read the room) and not burdening others with your problems. 괜찮은 척하다 (pretending to be fine) is not considered dishonest — it is considered polite, professional, and emotionally mature. If your boss asks how you're doing on a Monday morning and you are exhausted, the socially expected answer is 괜찮아요, not a detailed complaint. Similarly, 모르는 척하다 (pretending not to know) is often used by seniors to give juniors the space to present without the senior's greater knowledge overshadowing the room. Understand this cultural context and you'll find 척하다 appearing everywhere in Korean dramas, office stories, and everyday conversation — it's not always deception; it's often grace.

inlineExercises.prompt: 배가 안 고___ 척했어요. 사실 엄청 배고팠어요. (Adjective: 고프다 = to be hungry)
inlineExercises.explanation: 고프다 is an adjective, so it takes the adjective modifier -(으)ㄴ: 고픈 척했어요. If you chose -프는 척, that's the action-verb pattern (-는 척) applied to an adjective, which is the #1 척하다 mistake. Always check: adjective → -(으)ㄴ 척, verb → -는 척.

inlineExercises.prompt: 하마터면 지하철을 ___ 뻔했어요. (놓치다 = to miss a train)
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 uses the future/potential modifier -(으)ㄹ, not the present continuous -는. 놓치다 has a consonant-ending stem → -을 뻔했어요. 놓치는 뻔했어요 would be a completely different (and ungrammatical) construction.

inlineExercises.prompt: 답장이 없는 걸 보니까 바쁘___ 봐요. (바쁘다 = to be busy — adjective)
inlineExercises.explanation: 바쁘다 is an adjective → use -(으)ㄴ가 보다. If it were an action verb (e.g., 일하다), you'd use -나 봐요. 바쁜가 봐요 = I guess they're busy (based on the no-reply evidence). 바쁘나 봐요 is colloquially used and understood, but 바쁜가 봐요 is the textbook-correct form.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '발표할 뻔해요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Near-misses are finished events, so 뻔하다 must be in the past: 뻔했어요. 뻔해요 in the present would mean the near-miss is ongoing right now, which contradicts the logic of 뻔하다 — once you've ALMOST done something and DIDN'T, the moment is over.

inlineExercises.hint: 듣다 is an action verb. But you are pretending you ALREADY didn't hear — this is a past action, so use the past action modifier -(으)ㄴ: 들은 척. Add 못 before it for 'pretended not to have heard.'

inlineExercises.prompt: You notice your friend has been very quiet lately and you want to say 'I'm guessing something happened.' Which is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: 있다 is a stative verb (to exist/have) → use -나 봐요 for evidence-based inference. Option 1 (척해요) means PRETENDING something happened — totally different, implying your friend is faking. Option 3 (뻔했어요) means something ALMOST happened but didn't — also wrong; you're guessing it DID happen.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly says 'She pretended to be sick'?
inlineExercises.explanation: 아프다 is an adjective. Adjectives take -(으)ㄴ in modifier position: 아프 + 은 → 아픈. Option 1 (아프는 척) wrongly uses the action-verb pattern -는. Option 3 (아팠는 척) incorrectly attaches -는 to a past tense stem — neither 아팠는 nor 척하다 work that way. The correct and only natural form is 아픈 척했어요.

bullets: MASK (-는/-(으)ㄴ 척하다): put on a fake face — verb actions take -는 척, adjectives take -(으)ㄴ 척, past actions take -(으)ㄴ 척; 척하다 = deliberate pretense, not an honest impression
NEAR-MISS ALARM (-(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요): something almost happened but didn't — always past tense, add 하마터면 for drama, only with action verbs
EVIDENCE GUESS (-나 봐요 / -(으)ㄴ가 봐요): action verbs → -나 봐요, adjectives/이다 → -(으)ㄴ가 봐요; used for inferring about OTHER people from visible clues, not your own obvious feelings
